strengths: Addresses a practically important and timely question—when can weak, few-step, or domain-mismatched diffusion priors substitute for strong matched priors in inverse problems—that has been observed anecdotally in prior work but not systematically studied.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: multiple tasks (inpainting, Gaussian/nonlinear deblurring, super-resolution), multiple datasets (CelebA-HQ, LSUN Church/Bedroom, ImageNet), pixel- and latent-diffusion backbones (DDPM, Stable Diffusion 2.1, DiT), comparisons against several strong baselines (DPS, DMPlug, DAPS, DiffPIR, Deep Random Projector), noise-level sensitivity studies, compute-matched comparisons, and even scientific inverse problems from InverseBench.

Combines a clean theoretical narrative (classical posterior-consistency plus a tractable Gaussian-mixture surrogate with proven exponential concentration bounds) with a practical local spatial-autocorrelation diagnostic, giving two complementary and testable explanations for the phenomenon.

Honest and systematic study of failure modes (box inpainting, large-factor super-resolution, low measurement-informativeness regimes, high noise), including quantitative degradation curves and qualitative failure visualizations, rather than only reporting favorable cases.
Good reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters, dataset/checkpoint sources, and algorithmic details (AdamSphere, HoldoutTopK) are provided in the appendix, along with a stated code release.
The proposed AdamSphere optimizer and HoldoutTopK early-stopping rule are simple, well-motivated refinements with ablations isolating their individual contribution (Table 5).
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis (Theorem 3.2/Proposition A.5) is built on a linear-Gaussian, Gaussian-mixture surrogate model for the prior, which is a substantial simplification relative to the actual few-step DDIM/mismatched diffusion priors and nonlinear forward operators used in experiments; the connection between the formal theory and the realistic diffusion-sampling setting remains largely heuristic and is not rigorously bridged.

The main empirical comparisons contrast a strong-prior baseline solved with a full reverse-diffusion conditioning method (DPS) against weak priors solved with a different algorithm (initial-noise optimization, INO). This conflates the effect of prior strength with the effect of solver choice; the compute-matched comparison in Appendix C.11 shows INO requires 1.5–3x more compute than a single DPS run, which somewhat undercuts the 'weak priors are just as good' framing when compute is accounted for.

The 'identifiable score gap' assumption underlying the main theorem is close to tautological (it essentially requires that the correct candidate has a smaller residual than others) and is validated mainly for random inpainting; its applicability to the tested nonlinear or highly structured forward operators (nonlinear deblurring, super-resolution) is asserted more than rigorously demonstrated.

Reported PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS gaps between matched and mismatched/weak priors are sometimes non-trivial (e.g., CelebA inpainting 33.78 vs. 32.62 dB, CelebA super-resolution 31.27 vs. 30.10 dB, and larger gaps in the scientific inverse-problem experiments and DPS-mismatched-prior experiments in Appendix C.9), suggesting the 'nearly as well' claim is sometimes optimistic and depends heavily on task/domain choice.

The local spatial-autocorrelation diagnostic (Section 3.3) shows that short-range pixel correlations are similar across very different domains/sampler strengths, but this could be a fairly generic property of natural images (local smoothness) rather than a mechanism specific to diffusion priors; the causal link between this diagnostic and actual reconstruction success is argued informally rather than established quantitatively.

Statistical robustness of main results (e.g., variance across test images, significance of PSNR differences) is not consistently reported in the main tables, limiting confidence in the magnitude of reported gains versus baselines.

The paper's scope is limited to Gaussian-mixture-amenable, largely linear or mildly nonlinear inverse problems and image domains; results on scientific inverse problems (Appendix C.5) show noticeably larger matched-vs-mismatched gaps than natural images, which the authors acknowledge but which somewhat weakens the generality of the central claim.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and underexplored question: whether weak (few-step and/or domain-mismatched) diffusion priors suffice for inverse problems, going beyond anecdotal case studies in prior work to a more systematic treatment.

Combines a theoretical account (classical Bayesian posterior-consistency arguments plus an explicit, tractable Gaussian-mixture surrogate with proven exponential concentration rates) with a complementary empirical local spatial-autocorrelation diagnostic, giving two separate and mutually reinforcing explanations for the phenomenon.

Very extensive experimental validation: multiple tasks (inpainting, Gaussian/nonlinear deblurring, super-resolution), multiple datasets (CelebA-HQ, LSUN-Bedroom, LSUN-Church, ImageNet), multiple backbones (pixel-space DDPM, Stable Diffusion 2.1, DiT), comparisons against several strong baselines (DPS, DMPlug, DAPS, DiffPIR, Deep Random Projector), plus scientific inverse problems from InverseBench and sensitivity studies to measurement noise and compute budget — all in the appendix with considerable transparency.

Identifies and empirically/theoretically characterizes concrete failure regimes (large box inpainting, high-factor super-resolution, low effective measurement dimension), giving the paper a balanced and non-oversold narrative rather than claiming universal success of weak priors.

Reasonable reproducibility: hyperparameters, checkpoints, compute environment, and code link are provided, and ablations for the proposed AdamSphere optimizer and HoldoutTopK early-stopping rule are included.
weaknesses: The headline comparisons (e.g., Table 3) largely pit the authors' own solver (initial-noise optimization with AdamSphere + HoldoutTopK) under a weak prior against DPS under a strong prior; since solver and prior strength are varied simultaneously, it is hard to attribute gains purely to 'prior weakness being tolerable' rather than to the proposed optimization/early-stopping machinery itself. The solver-controlled ablation isolating domain mismatch alone (Appendix C.9, DPS with mismatched priors) is relegated to the appendix and is less emphasized than the main cross-method claims.

The theoretical model (linear measurement model + isotropic Gaussian-mixture prior surrogate) is a considerable simplification relative to actual k-step diffusion samplers and nonlinear forward operators used in the experiments; the key identifiability assumption (δ0-identifiable score gap) is only rigorously validated for random inpainting (Appendix A.4), leaving the applicability of the formal guarantees to deblurring, super-resolution, and nonlinear tasks largely heuristic.

Appendix C.11 shows that initial-noise optimization (INO) is 1.5–3× more compute-expensive than a single DPS run, and that compute-matched or best-of-several DPS runs can close or reverse the PSNR gap (e.g., DPS best-of-5 reaching 32.40 vs. INO's 31.86–34.13 depending on budget). This weakens the strength of the central empirical claim once computational cost is accounted for, even though the authors disclose this transparently.

Main result tables (e.g., Table 3, 4, 6) report point estimates without confidence intervals or variance across runs/seeds, making it difficult to assess whether the reported 0.1–2 dB PSNR differences are statistically meaningful, particularly since differences of this magnitude recur as central evidentiary claims throughout the paper.

The practically interesting regime for using strong generative priors — large missing regions, high-factor super-resolution, i.e., where hallucination/completion matters most — is precisely where weak priors are shown to fail; this narrows the practical scope of the paper's headline claim to data-rich regimes where simple reconstruction, not generative completion, is already comparatively easy, somewhat limiting the real-world significance of the main message despite its honest framing.

The theoretical sections are notation-heavy and the connection between the abstract Gaussian-mixture results and the concrete k-step DDIM/domain-mismatch 'two axes' framing used throughout the empirical sections is not always made explicit, making the paper's organizing logic harder to follow on a single read.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored question: when can weak/mismatched/few-step diffusion priors substitute for strong, domain-matched priors in inverse problems? This has direct relevance to data-scarce domains (e.g., medical/scientific imaging) where matched priors are unavailable.

Provides a genuinely complementary two-part explanation: (1) Bayesian posterior-consistency/concentration theory (Theorem 3.2 and its heterogeneous-variance generalization in Appendix A.3, plus a rigorous identifiability argument for random inpainting in Appendix A.5) showing that sufficiently informative measurements can make the posterior insensitive to the prior; and (2) an empirical local spatial-autocorrelation diagnostic showing that weak and strong natural-image priors share similar short-range structure, explaining why even mismatched priors propagate useful local information.

Extensive experimental validation across multiple tasks (inpainting, Gaussian/nonlinear deblurring, super-resolution), datasets (CelebA-HQ, LSUN-Church, LSUN-Bedroom, ImageNet), and backbones (DDPM, Stable Diffusion 2.1, DiT), plus a wide range of baselines (DPS, DMPlug, DAPS, DiffPIR, Deep Random Projector) and even scientific inverse problems from InverseBench (seismic/black-hole imaging), which strengthens the generality of the claims.

The paper does not only report positive results but systematically characterizes failure modes (box inpainting, high-factor super-resolution, high measurement noise) with both theoretical justification (the M·exp(-δ0 m) bound) and controlled experiments (Figure 4, Table 12, Table 16), giving a balanced and more credible picture.

Reasonably transparent about compute asymmetry between methods (Appendix C.11) and provides a compute-matched comparison showing the qualitative conclusion holds, which improves the soundness of the empirical claims.

The paper's algorithmic components (AdamSphere, HoldoutTopK) are simple, clearly explained, and shown via ablation to meaningfully help (Table 5), making the pipeline reasonably reproducible given the detailed experimental configuration in the appendix.
weaknesses: The core theoretical results rely on a finite Gaussian-mixture surrogate for the prior, which is a considerable idealization relative to actual k-step DDIM/latent diffusion priors used in experiments; the connection between the surrogate theory and the specific diffusion generators studied (e.g., 3-step DDIM, Stable Diffusion, DiT) is heuristic rather than formally established, so the theory functions more as an illustrative intuition-builder than a rigorous explanation of the empirical phenomenon.

Many of the headline PSNR/SSIM gains over DPS are modest (often well under 1 dB, e.g., Table 6, Table 15), and no variance/confidence intervals are reported for most main-text tables, making it hard to assess whether the reported improvements are statistically meaningful versus noise across the 100 test images.

The proposed method (initial-noise optimization with AdamSphere/HoldoutTopK) uses substantially more compute than DPS (1.5–3x per the authors' own accounting), and while a compute-matched ablation is provided in the appendix, the main-text comparisons in Section 4 are not compute-matched, which could overstate the practical competitiveness of weak priors relative to the strong-prior DPS baseline.

The core empirical observation that weak/mismatched/few-step diffusion priors can match strong priors is not entirely new (the paper itself cites Wang et al. 2024 and Jalal et al. 2021 reporting similar findings); the paper's main novel contribution is the systematic explanation and characterization of when/why this holds and fails, which is valuable but somewhat narrows the originality claim.

The paper is very long (37 pages) with a substantial fraction of the empirical substantiation (additional tasks, baselines, failure-mode details, scientific inverse problems, sensitivity analyses) relegated to the appendix; while thorough, this limits the self-containedness of the main text and places a burden on readers to verify central claims via appendix cross-referencing.

The 'δ0-identifiability' assumption underlying the main concentration theorem is somewhat abstract and only validated empirically for the specific case of random inpainting (Appendix A.4); its applicability to other tasks (deblurring, super-resolution) where the forward operator is not a simple coordinate projection is asserted but not similarly proven, leaving a gap between the formal theory and the breadth of tasks studied empirically.
